# OmniDB Documentation - Full Content

---

# Introduction
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/introduction.html

**Full Content:**

OmniDB is an open source browser-based app designed to access and manage many different Database Management systems: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, MS SQL Server, Firebird and SQLite. OmniDB can run either as a desktop app or via browser, combining the flexibility needed for various access paths with a design that puts security first. OmniDB is actively developed, automatically tested on a variety of databases and browsers and comes with full documentation.

Since early development, OmniDB was designed as a browser-based app. Consequently, it runs in any browser, from any operational system. It can be accessed by several computers and multiple users, each one of them with his/her own group of connections. It also can be hosted in any operational system, without the need of install any dependencies. We will see further details on installation in the next chapters.

OmniDB's main objective is to offer an unified workspace with all functionalities needed to manipulate different DMBS. DBMS specific tools aren't required: in OmniDB, the context switch between different DBMS is done with a simple connection switch, without leaving the same page. The end-user's sensation is that there is no difference when he/she manipulates different DBMS, it just feels like different connections.

Despite this, OmniDB is built with simplicity in mind, designed to be a fast and lightweight browser-based application. Long-running work — queries, procedures, and monitoring — is executed in the background and streamed back to the browser as it completes, so the user can keep working across multiple databases and multiple hosts at the same time without blocking on any single one.

OmniDB is also secure. Database passwords you choose to save are encrypted before they are stored, with a key kept in your operating system's secret store; if you prefer not to store a password at all, OmniDB asks for it when you connect and keeps it only in memory, for a limited time. A multi-user server adds sign-in protection and restricts what users can reach on the server machine itself — see Security and Multi-user Server.

Next to the SQL editor and the database tree, the workspace offers a live monitoring dashboard, a list of connected users, a notification listener (LISTEN/NOTIFY and friends), a role and privilege browser for PostgreSQL, snippets, data export to many formats and SSH terminals. The interface is available in English, Czech, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, Japanese and Korean — see Settings and Languages.

**History**

OmniDB's creators, Rafael Thofehrn Castro and William Ivanski, worked in a company where they needed to deal with several different databases from customers on a daily basis. These databases were from different DBMS technologies, and so they needed to keep switching between database management tools (typically one for each DBMS). As they were not keen of the existing unified database management tools (that could manage different DBMS), they came up with OmniDB's main idea.

OmniDB's first version was presented as an undergrad final project in the Computer Science Course from the Federal University of Paraná, in Brazil. The objective was to trace a common line between popular DBMS, and to study deeply their metadata. The result was a tool written in ASP.NET/C# capable of connecting and identifying the main structures (tables, keys, indexes and constraints), in a generic way, from several DBMS:

- Firebird
- MariaDB/MySQL
- Oracle
- PostgreSQL
- SQLite
- Microsoft SQL Server

OmniDB's first version also allowed the conversion between all DBMSs supported by the tool. This feature was developed to be user friendly, requiring just a few steps: the user needs to select a source connection, the structures that will be converted (just tables and all their structures, along with their data) and the target connection.

In 2025–2026, the project was revived with major releases (3.1.x), focusing on modernizing the codebase, improving security, and adding full support for modern operating systems like macOS Silicon, along with a complete documentation overhaul. This revival culminated in a full rewrite of the backend from Python/Django to Go (3.6.x), removing the Python runtime entirely and shipping a single native binary for every platform. See Legacy Features & History for the full version timeline and what changed along the way.

---

# Installation
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/installation.html

**Full Content:**

OmniDB provides 2 kinds of packages to fit every user needs:

- OmniDB Application: Runs a web server on a random port behind, and provides a simplified web browser window to use OmniDB interface without any additional setup. Just feels like a desktop application.
- OmniDB Server: Runs a web server on a random port, or a port specified by the user. User needs to connect to it through a web browser. Provides user management, ideal to be hosted on a server on users' networks.

Both application and server can be installed on the same machine.

**OmniDB Application**

Important: The original repository https://github.com/OmniDB/OmniDB/releases contains only old versions (up to ~2020) and is no longer maintained — see Legacy Features & History for what changed since.

For current versions use the project's releases page (https://github.com/heptau/omnidb/releases). Since the Go rewrite, every release is a single self-contained archive per platform (plus an optional installer for Windows) — no separate runtime to install first:

- macOS (Apple Silicon or Intel): [OmniDB-macOS-osx-arm64.zip](https://github.com/heptau/omnidb/releases/latest/download/OmniDB-macOS-osx-arm64.zip) / [OmniDB-macOS-osx-x64.zip](https://github.com/heptau/omnidb/releases/latest/download/OmniDB-macOS-osx-x64.zip)
- Linux x64: [OmniDB-linux-x64.tar.gz](https://github.com/heptau/omnidb/releases/latest/download/OmniDB-linux-x64.tar.gz)
- Windows x64: [OmniDB-win-x64.zip](https://github.com/heptau/omnidb/releases/latest/download/OmniDB-win-x64.zip), or the installer [OmniDB-win-x64-setup.exe](https://github.com/heptau/omnidb/releases/latest/download/OmniDB-win-x64-setup.exe)

Unzip (or untar) the archive for your platform and run the `OmniDB` app/binary inside — that's the whole install.

**Installation via Homebrew (macOS only – recommended)**

For macOS users who prefer using a package manager, OmniDB is available through a custom Homebrew tap:

```
# Install the latest version:
brew install --cask heptau/tap/omnidb
```

```
# To upgrade later:
brew upgrade heptau/tap/omnidb
```

Homebrew will automatically download the correct ZIP for your architecture (Apple Silicon or Intel), unzip it and place `OmniDB.app` into your Applications folder.

The cask definition is maintained here: heptau/homebrew-tap – omnidb.rb (https://github.com/heptau/homebrew-tap/blob/main/Casks/omnidb.rb)

**Installation via winget (Windows only)**

For Windows users who prefer using a package manager, OmniDB is available through the Windows Package Manager (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/package-manager/winget/), built into Windows 10 and 11:

```
# Install the latest version:
winget install heptau.OmniDB
```

```
# To upgrade later:
winget upgrade heptau.OmniDB
```

The manifest is maintained here: microsoft/winget-pkgs (https://github.com/microsoft/winget-pkgs/tree/master/manifests/h/heptau/OmniDB).

**Direct download (all platforms)**

- macOS (Apple Silicon) (https://github.com/heptau/omnidb/releases/latest/download/OmniDB-macOS-osx-arm64.zip)
- macOS (Intel) (https://github.com/heptau/omnidb/releases/latest/download/OmniDB-macOS-osx-x64.zip)
- Linux (x64) (https://github.com/heptau/omnidb/releases/latest/download/OmniDB-linux-x64.tar.gz)
- Windows (x64) (https://github.com/heptau/omnidb/releases/latest/download/OmniDB-win-x64.zip)
- Windows (x64) installer (https://github.com/heptau/omnidb/releases/latest/download/OmniDB-win-x64-setup.exe)

These links always point to the latest release. For older versions, checksums, and release notes, see the releases page (https://github.com/heptau/omnidb/releases).

Unzip the archive for your platform and launch the app the normal way: on macOS, drag `OmniDB.app` into Applications and open it from Launchpad/Spotlight or `open -a OmniDB`; on Linux, run the `OmniDB` binary directly; on Windows, run `OmniDB.exe` (or the installer).

See Desktop App for where the app keeps its data, its menu bar and keyboard shortcuts, and macOS specifics such as importing data from an earlier installation.

**OmniDB Server**

The same release archive also contains `omnidb-server` — a separate, headless binary alongside the desktop app (the desktop app actually launches this same binary internally, as a child process, forcing app mode). Run it directly for the browser-accessible server mode, with no desktop shell involved:

```
user@machine:~$ ./omnidb-server
omnidb-server: listening on 127.0.0.1:52149 — open http://127.0.0.1:52149/omnidb_login/ in your browser
```

By default OmniDB listens on `127.0.0.1` only and picks a free port automatically. You can specify both explicitly:

```
user@machine:~$ ./omnidb-server -p 8080 -H 0.0.0.0
omnidb-server: listening on 0.0.0.0:8080 — open http://0.0.0.0:8080/omnidb_login/ in your browser
```

See Deploying omnidb-server for the full set of options and recommended deployment setups (in particular, why exposing `-H 0.0.0.0` directly to the internet without a reverse proxy in front is discouraged — there's no built-in TLS support).

**OmniDB with Oracle**

Neither OmniDB app nor server require any additional software to connect to Oracle — unlike previous releases, no separate Oracle Instant Client installation is needed. Oracle connectivity is implemented natively (a pure Go driver), so it works the same way out of the box as every other supported database. The same is true for MS SQL Server and Firebird: both also use pure Go drivers, so no ODBC driver, native client library, or other extra install step is required for either of them.

**OmniDB User Database**

Upon first run, both server and app create a file `~/.omnidb/omnidb-app/omnidb.db` (for OmniDB app) or `~/.omnidb/omnidb-server/omnidb.db` (for OmniDB server) in the user home directory, if it does not exist yet — along with an `admin` superuser account. The desktop app signs in as this user automatically; in server mode its password is randomly generated and printed once to the server's log output (the line containing `initial login: admin / …`). This file is also called the user database and contains all users, connections, and other application data. If it already exists (e.g. after an upgrade), OmniDB uses it as-is — it is never overwritten or reset automatically.

**OmniDB in the browser**

Once `omnidb-server` is running, open the address it printed on startup (for example `http://127.0.0.1:52149/omnidb_login/`) in your favorite browser. You will see OmniDB's sign-in page; sign in as `admin` with the one-time password from the log. In the next chapters, we will see how to create users and connections and how to work with OmniDB. The desktop app skips this step entirely — it opens the workspace directly.

---

# Desktop App
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/desktop_app.html

**Full Content:**

The desktop app (`OmniDB.app` on macOS, `OmniDB`/`OmniDB.exe` on Linux and Windows) is a small native window around the same OmniDB interface the server version serves to browsers. It starts its own private copy of `omnidb-server` in the background, listening on the local machine only, and signs you in automatically as the built-in `admin` user — there is no sign-in page, no Account icon and nothing to configure. See Installation for how to get it.

**Where the data lives**

Saved connections, snippets, settings, query history and so on are kept in `~/.omnidb/omnidb-app/` (the `omnidb.db` user database, plus a `temp` folder for exports and the saved window position). To keep a separate set of data — for example a throwaway one for testing — start the app with a different home directory:

```
open -a OmniDB --args -d /path/to/other/dir    # macOS
./OmniDB -d /path/to/other/dir                  # Linux
OmniDB.exe -d C:\path\to\other\dir              # Windows
```

The directory must already exist; a new, empty one is set up automatically on first use. Saved passwords are encrypted with a key kept in the operating system's secret store — see Security and Multi-user Server.

**The menu bar**

- OmniDB: About OmniDB, Settings… (Cmd/Ctrl-,), Import Data from Previous Installation… (sandboxed macOS build only, see below) and Quit OmniDB (Cmd/Ctrl-Q).
- Edit and Window: the operating system's standard menus (undo/cut/copy/paste, minimize, zoom, full screen, …).
- View: jump to a section of the left rail — Welcome (Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-W), Connections (Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-C), Database (Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-D), Notify (Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-N), Connected Users (Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-U), Snippets (Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-S) — plus Toggle Database Tree (Cmd/Ctrl-B) and Toggle Properties/DDL Panel (Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-B).
- Help: Getting Started (the interactive tutorial), Keyboard Shortcuts (opens Settings on the Shortcuts category), Visit omnidb.net and GitHub Repository.

The OmniDB, View and Help menus are shown in the language chosen under Settings > Appearance > Language and switch as soon as you change it; before the first page has loaded they follow the operating system's language. The standard Edit and Window menus stay in English. The window title shows the section you are in (for example OmniDB - Snippets).

**Window size and position**

On its very first launch the window opens maximized. After that it reopens with the size, position and maximized/restored state it had when you last closed it.

**Links and files**

Links to external pages (the Doc: … entries of the database tree, the Welcome page's links, the Help menu) open in your default web browser. Exports and Export as DBML open the native Save As dialog, so you choose where the file goes directly — see Writing SQL Queries.

**macOS: sandbox, previous data and `.pgpass`**

The macOS app runs in the App Sandbox, which gives it its own private home folder. Two consequences:

- Data from an earlier, non-sandboxed install in `~/.omnidb` is not visible automatically. On the first launch without any data, OmniDB offers to import it — choose Import… and pick your previous `.omnidb` folder, or Not Now. You can do the same later with OmniDB > Import Data from Previous Installation….
- `~/.pgpass` is not readable until you allow it. When a PostgreSQL connection has no stored password, the password prompt offers Grant access to .pgpass…: pick your `.pgpass` file once (hidden files are shown in that dialog) and OmniDB remembers the permission, so every later PostgreSQL connection looks its password up there, just as `psql` would. Import connections from .pgpass… in the Connections section grants the same access. See Creating Users and Connections.

---

# Creating Users and Connections
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/creating_users_and_connections.html

**Full Content:**

**Logging in as user admin**

OmniDB comes only with the user admin. If you are using the server version, the first thing to do is sign in as admin with the one-time random password that `omnidb-server` printed to its log output when it created a new app database (the line containing `initial login: admin / …`), and then change it under Settings. If that password gets lost, reset it with `omnidb-server --set-password admin`. After 10 failed sign-in attempts for the same username or client IP address, sign-in is locked for 15 minutes. The desktop app has no sign-in at all — it runs as a single local user, so everything about user management below simply does not appear there.

**Finding your way around**

The whole workspace is reached from the vertical icon rail on the left edge of the window: Welcome, Connections (the plug), Database, Monitoring, Notify, Permissions, Connected Users and Snippets at the top, and Getting Started, Account (server version only) and Settings (the cog) at the bottom. Hovering an icon shows its name. See Managing Databases for how the sections work together, and Settings and Languages for the interface language and other preferences.

**Creating another user**

Open Settings at the bottom of the rail and pick the Account category, then click Manage Users. Only a super user has that button — a regular user's Settings has no Account section at all.

The User management window lists the existing users. Click Add new user (the person-with-plus icon) to insert a new, blank user row, shown as (pending info) until you fill it in. Fill in the User name and New password, switch on Superuser? if the new user should be one, and click Save. You can create as many users as you want, edit existing ones, and delete a user by clicking the red cross in the actions column.

To sign out, click the Account icon (the person, near the bottom of the rail) and then Sign out.

Deleting a user, or taking away superuser status, takes effect immediately, including for that user's sessions that are already open.

**The Connections section**

Click the plug icon in the rail. Connections are a full section of the workspace, not a popup: a master–detail split view with the list of saved connections in the sidebar on the left and the selected connection's own form and buttons on the right.

Each row in the list shows the database engine's icon, the connection's name, and below it the `user@server:port` it points at (or the connection string, or the SSH target for a terminal connection). A small colored dot marks the connection's environment, and a key icon marks one that goes through an SSH tunnel.

**Creating connections**

OmniDB supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, MS SQL Server, Firebird and SQLite, plus a Terminal connection type that opens an SSH shell instead of a database. The Connection Type list shows PostgreSQL first, then the others alphabetically, and Terminal last.

For SQLite, the connection points at a database file (on the machine where `omnidb-server` runs); if the file does not exist yet, Test Connection says so and the file is created when you first use the connection. On a multi-user server, SQLite connections are reserved for superusers, and some PostgreSQL connection-string parameters that read files on the server are rejected — see Security and Multi-user Server.

Click the + button under the list to create a connection. Type its name into the heading of the form on the right, choose the Connection Type, and fill in the Host Connection Info card: Server, Port, Database, User and, optionally, User Password. Instead of those individual fields you can fill in a single Connection string (for example `postgresql://postgres@localhost:5432/postgres`) and leave the rest blank. When you are done, click Save in the top right corner of the form.

Test Connection next to it tries the connection without opening it and reports either Connection successful. or the exact error the database returned. The − button under the list deletes the selected connection; it stays disabled for a connection that is currently open in a tab.

**Passwords**

The User Password field is optional, and the two choices behave differently:

- Filled in: the password is saved into OmniDB's own configuration database and used automatically every time you open the connection. It is encrypted (AES-256-GCM) before being written to that database file, using a key kept in your operating system's own secret store (Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, Secret Service on Linux) rather than inside the file itself — so the database file alone is no longer enough to read the passwords in it. If no such secret store is available, OmniDB falls back to a key file kept alongside the database.
- Left blank: nothing is stored, and OmniDB asks for the password when you open the connection. What you type is kept only in the server's memory, for your session and that connection, for 30 minutes — after that OmniDB asks again.

For PostgreSQL, OmniDB also looks the password up in your `.pgpass` file at connect time, matching the same entry libpq would, so a connection with no stored password can still open without a prompt. In the sandboxed macOS app the password prompt offers Grant access to .pgpass…: you point at the file once and every later connection resolves its own password from it.

If the database refuses the attempt, the prompt stays on screen showing the error OmniDB got (fe_sendauth: no password supplied, an authentication failure, a server that is down, and so on), so you can correct the password and try again.

**Importing connections from `.pgpass`**

The file-import icon next to the + and − buttons reads a `.pgpass` file and creates one PostgreSQL connection per concrete line in it, as a bare `postgresql://user@host:port/db` connection string with no password stored — the point being to keep authenticating from that file rather than copying passwords into OmniDB. Wildcard (`*`) lines are skipped, and so is any line that already matches an existing connection.

**Organizing the list**

- Order: drag a row to any slot in the list. The arrangement is stored per user and survives a reload and a restart. Connections you create later are added at the bottom.
- Groups: the selector at the top of the sidebar filters the list down to one group. + Group creates a group, and the … button next to it offers Rename, Manage Connections (turns the rows into checkboxes so you can pick which connections belong to the group, then Save changes) and Delete.
- Public connections: the Public connection? switch in the form makes a connection usable by every other OmniDB user. Only its owner can edit it; other users never see its saved password (a password inside its connection string is masked for them), and their Test Connection always tests the stored server. The Public (n) switch at the bottom of the sidebar shows or hides other users' public connections in your own list.
- Environment: tagging a connection Production, UAT, Development or Archive colors its dot in the list and the edge of its open tab — mainly a safety cue, so reaching for the wrong tab is visibly obvious.

**Opening a connection**

Click Connect in the form, or simply double-click a row in the list, and OmniDB opens it in a new Connection Outer Tab as we can see in the next chapter. Right-clicking a row opens a context menu (Connect/Edit/Delete — Delete is omitted for a connection that is already open), and right-clicking empty space in the list offers New Connection/Refresh.

**Using SSH tunnels**

OmniDB allows the user to connect to any remote database through SSH tunnels. Tick Use SSH tunnel in the connection's own form — that enables the fields below it:

- SSH Server: The server you are connecting to via SSH. Its host key must already be in the `~/.ssh/known_hosts` file of the operating-system user running OmniDB, otherwise the tunnel is refused — see Security and Multi-user Server;
- SSH Port: The port of the SSH server (default is 22, but it can be any port number);
- SSH User: The operating system user name you use to connect to the SSH server;
- Password/Passphrase: The password of the operating system user (or the passphrase for the key below). Leave it blank and OmniDB asks for it each time the tunnel is opened, without storing it. If you fill the field SSH Key Text File, a password is optional;
- SSH Key Text File: The contents of the local private SSH key you can use to connect to the SSH server. OmniDB reads the file you pick and stores its text, not the file itself. If you fill this field, then you can also fill the field Password/Passphrase, but in this case it will be the passphrase for the SSH private key.

Everything you do store here — the SSH password, the passphrase and the key text — is kept in the same local OmniDB configuration database as the database passwords, encrypted the same way.

While using SSH tunnels, you also need to fill all database fields accordingly. But instead of being relative to the OmniDB server, they will be relative to the SSH Server. This can be done in 2 scenarios as explained below.

If the database is inside the same server as you are connecting to via SSH, then you will have a situation like this:

In this scenario, the database Server will be `127.0.0.1`, as the database is in the same machine as the SSH Server.

But the database can be outside the SSH server, like this:

Here the database Server needs to be `192.168.0.10`, as it is the relative address for the SSH server to connect to the database server.

---

# Settings and Languages
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/settings_and_languages.html

**Full Content:**

Every OmniDB user has their own preferences: interface language, theme, font size, export options, autocomplete categories, SQL formatting style and keyboard shortcuts. They are all set in Settings and stored per user in OmniDB's user database, so they follow you to any browser or machine where you sign in to the same OmniDB server.

**Opening Settings**

Click the cog icon at the bottom of the left rail. In the desktop app you can also use the menu bar's OmniDB > Settings… (Cmd-, on macOS, Ctrl-, elsewhere), and Help > Keyboard Shortcuts opens Settings directly on the Shortcuts category.

Settings is a two-pane view: categories on the left (Appearance, Export, Autocomplete, Formatting, Shortcuts, Password and, for superusers only, Account) and the selected category's fields on the right. There is no Save button — every field is saved as soon as you change it (text fields shortly after you stop typing). The only exception is the password, which has its own Change Password button.

**Appearance**

- Language: the language of the whole user interface — Automatic, Čeština, Deutsch, English, Español, Français, Italiano, Português, 日本語 (Japanese) or 한국어 (Korean). Automatic (the default) follows the language your browser or operating system asks for, and falls back to English if that language is not available. Changing the language reloads the page. The same applies to the sign-in page, and in the desktop app to the menu bar (see Desktop App). Names of database engines, file formats and character encodings, SQL keywords and messages coming from the database server itself are not translated.
- Theme: Automatic (follows the operating system's light/dark setting, and switches live when it changes), Light or Dark.
- Font Size: a slider from 10 to 20 (default 12) scaling the interface text; the current value is shown next to it.

**Export**

- CSV/TSV Encoding: the character encoding of CSV and TSV exports, grouped into Unicode, Windows codepages, ISO 8859, Cyrillic, East Asian, DOS, Mac and EBCDIC encodings. The default is UTF-8 with BOM, which spreadsheet applications such as Excel recognize as UTF-8 automatically.
- CSV Delimiter: the field separator used for CSV exports (default `;`).

See Writing SQL Queries for exporting query results.

**Autocomplete**

Autocomplete Suggestions chooses which categories the SQL editor's autocomplete offers: Keywords, Databases, Roles, Tablespaces, Schemas, Extensions, Tables, Views, Columns, Functions and Indexes (All/None toggle them all at once).

**Formatting**

These options control how Indent SQL (the formatter in Query tabs and the Indent button in Snippets) rewrites your SQL, and how the SQL templates generated from the database tree are laid out:

- Indent Character: Spaces (default) or Tab;
- Indent Size: 2, 3 or 4 (default 4);
- Comma Style: Leading (, at line start) (default) or Trailing (, at line end);
- Keyword Case: Preserve (default), UPPERCASE or lowercase;
- Ruler Column: where every SQL editor draws its vertical guide line (24–999, default 128). It is a visual guide only; the formatter does not wrap lines at it.

**Shortcuts**

OmniDB's own keyboard shortcuts, in two groups. To change one, click its button, press the new key combination, or press Esc to cancel. The defaults are:

| Action | Windows/Linux | Mac |
|---|---|---|
| Database (Query and Console tabs) |
| Run Query | Alt-Q | Ctrl-Q |
| Run Explain | Alt-W | Ctrl-W |
| Run Explain Analyze | Alt-E | Ctrl-E |
| Cancel Query | Alt-C | Ctrl-C |
| Indent | Alt-S | Ctrl-S |
| Autocomplete | Ctrl-Space | Option-Space |
| New Inner Tab | Alt-I | Ctrl-I |
| Remove Current Inner Tab | Alt-Shift-Q | Ctrl-Shift-Q |
| Select Left Inner Tab | Alt-O | Ctrl-O |
| Select Right Inner Tab | Alt-P | Ctrl-P |
| Snippets (Snippets section) |
| Save Snippet | Ctrl-S | Command-S |
| New Snippet | Ctrl-N | Command-N |
| Close Snippet Tab | Ctrl-W | Command-W |

The text-editing shortcuts of the SQL editor itself (selection, multiple cursors, folding, find & replace, …) are listed separately in Editor Keyboard Shortcuts. The desktop app's menu bar adds shortcuts for switching sections (see Desktop App).

**Password**

Type the New Password and repeat it in Confirm; Change Password becomes available once both match. Changing your password signs out your other sessions. This category is only useful in server mode — the desktop app signs in automatically.

**Account**

Shown to superusers only: Manage Users opens the User management window where OmniDB users are added, edited and removed — see Creating Users and Connections.

---

# Managing Databases
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/managing_databases.html

**Full Content:**

After creating a connection you can open it by clicking Connect in the Connections section, or by double-clicking it in the connection list. OmniDB then switches to the Database section and opens the connection in a new connection tab.

**Sections of the workspace**

The icon rail on the left edge of the window switches between the workspace's sections:

- Welcome: the start page, with links to the documentation and the Getting started tutorial (see Additional Features);
- Connections: where connections are created, arranged and opened (see Creating Users and Connections);
- Database: the open connection tabs, each with its database tree and its Query and Console tabs — described in this chapter;
- Monitoring, Notify, Permissions and Connected Users: tools that work on the connections open in the Database section (see Monitoring Dashboard, Notify, Roles and Permissions and Connected Users);
- Snippets: your saved pieces of SQL (see Snippets);
- at the bottom, Getting Started (the interactive tutorial), Account (server version only: the current user, the version and Sign out) and Settings (see Settings and Languages; superusers also find Manage Users there).

The Database, Monitoring, Notify, Permissions and Connected Users sections all show the same strip of open connection tabs at the top, with the same selection: select a connection in one of them and the others follow. Switching sections never closes a connection.

**Connection tabs**

Each open connection is a tab in that strip, named after the connection. A connection tagged with an environment (Production, UAT, Development, Archive) shows that environment's color on its tab, so a production connection is easy to tell apart. Hovering a tab shows its details (server, or connection string), and hovering reveals its close button (×). Tabs can be reordered by dragging them.

The + at the end of the strip opens another connection: it lists your saved connections (grouped, if you use groups) and, under SSH Consoles, your terminal connections. Closing a connection tab ends its database sessions.

Inside a connection tab you find:

- The database tree on the left, where you navigate through the database objects. Right-clicking a node shows what you can do with it.
- The Properties and DDL panels below the tree, showing the properties and the `CREATE` statement of the node selected in the tree. The tree and this panel can be resized by dragging their dividers and collapsed with the small toggle buttons on them.
- Inner tabs on the right. The + at the end of the inner tab strip adds a Query Tab or a Console Tab; other actions (such as Edit Data on a table) open their own inner tabs.

A Query Tab contains an SQL Editor with syntax highlighting, autocomplete and find & replace, a toolbar (Run, Run Statement at Cursor, Indent SQL, Command history, Explain, Explain Analyze, Autocommit, Export Data, …) and the results area below it with the Data, Messages and Explain subtabs. See Writing SQL Queries for the details.

**Working with databases**

Expand the root node of the tree (named after the database engine). The first time you use a connection whose password is not stored, OmniDB asks for it. A password typed into that prompt is remembered for 30 minutes of your session; after that the prompt appears again. After you type the correct password, the root node shows the server version and expands, showing the current database connection and also instance-wide elements — for PostgreSQL: Databases, Tablespaces, Roles and Replication Slots.

You can connect to a single PostgreSQL database, and using the same connection you can connect to other databases in the same PostgreSQL instance. To switch, expand the node of another database: OmniDB asks whether you really want to change the active database, and on Yes makes it the active database of that connection tab.

Go ahead and expand the Schemas node. You will see all schemas in the current database (in case of PostgreSQL, `TOAST` and temp schemas are not shown).

Now click to expand the schema `public`. You will see different kinds of elements contained in this schema.

Now click to expand the node Tables, and you will see all tables contained in the schema `public`. Expand any table and you will see its columns, primary key, foreign keys, constraints, indexes, rules, triggers and partitions.

In order to view records inside a table, right click it and choose Data Actions > Query Data.

Notice that OmniDB opens a new SQL editor with a simple query to list table records. The records are displayed in a grid right below the editor. This grid can be controlled with keyboard as if you were using a spreadsheet manager. You can also copy data from single cells or block of cells (that can be selected with the keyboard or mouse) and paste on any spreadsheet manager.

You can edit the query on the SQL editor, writing simple or more complex queries. To execute, click on the Run button or press `Alt-Q` (`Ctrl-Q` on macOS). If the result has more rows than the first batch fetched, the buttons Fetch more and Fetch all appear. More details in the next chapters.

**Working with multiple tabs inside the same connection**

Inside a single connection, you can create several inner tabs by clicking on the + at the end of the inner tab strip, and then choosing Query Tab (or Console Tab).

On OmniDB, you can execute several SQL statements and procedures in parallel. Each Query Tab has its own database session. While a tab is executing, a spinner is shown on it; when a tab you are not looking at finishes, it shows a checkmark instead. The red Cancel button cancels the statement running in the current tab.

You can also drag and drop a tab to change its order. This works with both inner tabs and connection tabs. When a row of tabs runs out of room, the tabs shrink step by step down to icon-only; hovering an icon-only tab shows its name.

Additionally, you can use keyboard shortcuts to manage inner tabs. These are the defaults on Windows/Linux (macOS uses Ctrl instead of Alt); all of them can be changed under Settings > Shortcuts:

- Alt-I: Insert a new inner tab
- Alt-Shift-Q: Removes the current inner tab
- Alt-O: Change focus to inner tab at left
- Alt-P: Change focus to inner tab at right

There are no keyboard shortcuts for connection tabs — use the mouse or drag-and-drop for those. (The desktop app's View menu has shortcuts for switching sections; see Desktop App.)

All Query tabs are saved automatically whenever you execute them. Even if you close the OmniDB window or browser tab, they are stored in OmniDB's user database and restored the next time you open OmniDB (in the desktop app) or sign in again (in the server version) — OmniDB then starts in the Database section with those connections open. Closing a connection tab or an inner tab yourself deletes it permanently, so it will not be restored.

---

# Creating, Changing and Removing Tables
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/creating_changing_and_removing_tables.html

**Full Content:**

Table structures — creating, altering and dropping — are managed with editable SQL templates rather than a graphical form. This gives you more direct control than a point-and-click designer, at the cost of writing a little SQL yourself: OmniDB fills in a working starting template and you edit it before running it.

**Creating tables**

We will create example tables (customers and addresses) in the `testdb` database we connected to earlier. Right click on the Tables node and select the Create Table action. This opens a new Query tab pre-filled with a `CREATE TABLE` template for the current schema.

Edit the template into the table you actually want — for customers, a primary key that addresses will later reference:

```
CREATE TABLE public.customers (
	cust_id serial PRIMARY KEY,
	cust_name varchar(100) NOT NULL
);
```

Run the statement (the same way you run any query). Right-click the Tables tree node and click Refresh — the new table now appears under it. Keeping customers selected in the tree, you can inspect its generated Properties and DDL in the panel beside the tree, the same panel used for every other object type.

Now create addresses, with a foreign key back to customers:

```
CREATE TABLE public.addresses (
	add_id serial PRIMARY KEY,
	add_street varchar(200) NOT NULL,
	add_number integer,
	cust_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES public.customers (cust_id)
);
```

At this point there are two related tables in schema `public`. You can see the schema structure with the graph feature: right click the schema `public` node and select Render Graph > Simple Graph for just the tables and their relationships, or Render Graph > Complete Graph to also include columns and constraints. Both render as an interactive, pannable/zoomable diagram.

**Altering tables**

To change an existing table — say, adding a column to customers — right click the table node and select Table Actions > Alter Table. This opens a Query tab with an `ALTER TABLE` template you edit and run, the same pattern as table creation:

```
ALTER TABLE public.customers ADD COLUMN cust_age integer;
```

Any error the database returns — for example trying to add a column name that already exists — shows up the same way any failed query does: in the query tab's Messages panel, with the exact command and error text from the database.

**Removing tables**

To drop a table, right click the table node and select Table Actions > Drop Table. This, too, opens an editable template (`DROP TABLE ...`) rather than dropping immediately — review it and run it when you're ready.

---

# Managing Table Data
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/managing_table_data.html

**Full Content:**

The tool allows us to edit records contained in tables through a very simple and intuitive interface. Given that only a few DBMS automatically provide a unique identifier for table records, we opted to allow data editing and removal only for tables that have a primary key. Tables that do not have it can only receive new records.

To access the record editing interface, right click the table node and select the action Data Actions > Edit Data:

The Edit Data tab has a small SQL editor for an optional filter and ordering clause, appended to the query that loads the records — for example `where t.cust_id > 10 order by t.cust_name` (the table is available under the alias `t`) — a drop-down that limits how many records are loaded (Query 10 rows, Query 100 rows or Query 1000 rows) and a Run button that (re)loads the grid. The records grid has column names and data types. Columns that belong to the primary key have a key icon next to their names. If the table has no primary key, OmniDB warns Table has no primary key, existing rows will be read only. — you can still add new rows.

Changes are not written immediately: edit, add and mark rows as needed, then click Save Changes, which appears as soon as there is something to save. The first column of each row holds its row action: clicking the × there marks the row for deletion (click again to undo), or removes a new, not yet saved row.

The row of the grid that have the symbol `+` is the row to add new records. Let us insert some records in the table `customers`:

After saving, the records will be inserted and can be edited (only because this table has a primary key). Let's change the cust_name of some of the existing records and, at the same time, let's remove one of the rows:

Tables can have fields with values represented by very long strings. To help edit these fields, right-click the cell and choose Edit Content: a larger editor opens (with syntax highlighting for JSON/JSONB and XML columns), and Save writes the value back into the grid. The same menu has Copy:

The interface detects errors that may occur during operations related to records. To demonstrate, let us insert two records with existing `cust_id` (primary key):

It shows which commands tried to be executed and the respective errors.

To complete this chapter, let's add some records to the Address table:

# Writing SQL Queries
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/writing_sql_queries.html

**Full Content:**

The most common kind of inner tab is the Query Tab, containing the following elements. Keyboard shortcuts below are the Windows/Linux defaults; on macOS, OmniDB's own shortcuts use Ctrl instead of Alt. All of them can be changed under Settings > Shortcuts.

- 1) Tab Header: You can see the name of the tab and, on hover, an icon to close it. While a query is running in the tab you will see a spinner; if it finishes while you are working on a different tab, a checkmark is shown. Right-clicking the tab and choosing Rename Tab lets you rename it.
- 2) Add Tab: You can quickly add another inner tab (Query Tab or Console Tab) by clicking on the plus icon.
- 3) SQL Editor: Full-featured SQL editor with SQL syntax highlighting, code folding, Find & Replace (`Ctrl-F` and `Ctrl-H`), a vertical ruler line (its column is set under Settings > Formatting) and an autocomplete component, explained below. Right-clicking in the editor offers Copy, Save as snippet and Use snippet (see Snippets). See Editor Keyboard Shortcuts for the full list of editor shortcuts (selection, multicursor, navigation, folding, etc.).
- 4) Run: The text contained in the SQL Editor will be executed against the current active database when you click on this button (or press `Alt-Q`). If there is some selected text in the SQL Editor, only the selected text is executed. The editor may contain several statements separated by semicolons; they run one after another and the grid shows the result of the last one. Once the command is running, a red Cancel button is shown, allowing you to cancel the execution (or press `Alt-C`).
- 5) Run Statement at Cursor: Runs only the single statement the cursor is in, without having to select it first. With the cursor right after a `;`, the following statement is run.
- 6) Indent SQL: This button will prettify any SQL code written in the SQL editor (shortcut `Alt-S`), following the style chosen under Settings > Formatting (indentation, comma style, keyword case).
- 7) Command history: All commands executed against the current connection are stored in the command history, which can be accessed by clicking on this button. You can filter it by date range and by text to find the SQL command you need.
- 8) Explain (PostgreSQL only): Runs your SQL query with `EXPLAIN` in front of it (shortcut `Alt-W`). The results will be shown in a textual and graphical form in the Explain tab (please see Visualizing Query Plans for more details).
- 9) Explain Analyze (PostgreSQL only): Same as Explain button, but runs the SQL query with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, which will effectively execute the query (shortcut `Alt-E`).
- 10) Autocommit (PostgreSQL only): When enabled, every query executed will be committed to the database. When disabled, OmniDB starts a transaction and upon execution of a query, the interface will show buttons allowing the user to Commit or Rollback. The user can also keep the transaction open and execute other commands.
- 11) Backend Status (PostgreSQL only): When you open a new Query Tab, the status is Not connected, because OmniDB didn't start a PostgreSQL backend yet. When you execute the first query, OmniDB starts a new backend and keeps it linked to the Query Tab (each Query Tab gets its own backend). The status of the backend (Idle, Running, Idle in transaction, etc.) will be shown in this field. When you close the Query Tab, OmniDB terminates the backend.
- 12) Export File Type: CSV, TSV, XLSX, JSON, XML or Markdown.
- 13) Export Data: By clicking on this button, OmniDB executes the current query and exports the whole result to a file of the chosen type. In the desktop app, a native Save As dialog opens so you can choose where to save it directly, and OmniDB confirms with File exported to: …. When running as a browser-based OmniDB Server instead, the file is written to the server's temp folder first, and the result area then shows The file is ready. with a Save link that downloads it through the browser. CSV/TSV encoding and the CSV delimiter are set under Settings > Export.
- 14) Data Results: If the query is a `SELECT`, then it will show a grid with the results; the first column stays pinned while you scroll horizontally, and hovering a column header shows its full name. If the query is a DML or DDL, it will show the message returned by the RDBMS. When there are more rows than the first batch, Fetch more loads the next batch and Fetch all the rest. Right-click a cell for Copy or View Content; JSON and XML values are shown syntax-highlighted.
- 15) Messages (PostgreSQL only): Any messages (such as the ones given by the command `RAISE NOTICE`) will be shown here.
- 16) Explain View (PostgreSQL only): Shows a full-featured component to view the PostgreSQL execution plan in textual or graphical form.

The divider between the editor (with its toolbar) and the results can be dragged to give either more room.

**Safety confirmation for destructive statements**

Before running a statement that starts with `DROP` or `TRUNCATE`, or an `UPDATE`/`DELETE` without a `WHERE` clause, the Query Tab asks for confirmation (This statement is destructive and cannot be undone. Run it anyway?, or This statement has no WHERE clause and will affect ALL rows. Run it anyway?). This is a safety net against honest mistakes, not a permission system — it looks only at the beginning of the text (after comments).

Once executed, the tabs are also saved in OmniDB user database (title and contents), so the next time you open OmniDB, you will see them all open. Also, every command you execute in a Query Tab is saved to the command history of that connection.

**SQL Autocomplete**

The SQL editor has a feature that helps a lot when creating new queries: SQL code completion. Open the suggestions with `Ctrl-Space` (`Option-Space` on macOS). With this feature it is possible to autocomplete columns contained in a table referenced by an alias: type the alias, the character `.` and then open the autocomplete:

If the user does not start the autocomplete with the cursor close to a table alias, the component will show multiple categories of data. By typing in the filter textbox, elements in all categories will be filtered:

The autocomplete component is also able to identify some contextual information. For example, if you type a name of a schema, then type the character `.`, you will be able to filter among objects contained only in that schema:

After `::` (a PostgreSQL type cast), only data types are offered. Choosing a keyword also adds what always follows it (for example a space after `SELECT`, or the opening parenthesis after `COALESCE`). Which categories are offered at all (keywords, databases, roles, tablespaces, schemas, extensions, tables, views, columns, functions, indexes) is set under Settings > Autocomplete.

Please note that for RDBMS other than PostgreSQL, the autocomplete component only works for table columns.

---

# Snippets
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/snippets.html

**Full Content:**

Snippets are pieces of text — queries, scripts, command templates, notes — that you keep in OmniDB and reuse from any SQL editor. They are organized in a folder tree, stored in OmniDB's own user database (so they survive upgrades) and private to each OmniDB user.

**The Snippets section**

Click the Snippets icon (the scroll) in the left rail. The section shows the folder tree on the left and snippet editor tabs on the right; the divider between them can be dragged.

Right-click empty space in the tree for Refresh, New Folder and Add Snippet. Right-clicking a folder offers the same plus Rename Folder and Delete Folder; right-clicking a snippet offers Edit, Rename and Delete. Double-clicking a snippet opens it in an editor tab (or switches to it, if it is already open). The + button below the tree adds a snippet to the selected folder (or at the top level), and − deletes the selected item.

**Editing and saving**

Each editor tab is a full SQL editor (syntax highlighting, autocomplete, find & replace) with Indent and Save buttons below it. The section always starts with one empty New Snippet tab, and the + tab opens another one.

A small dot next to a tab's title means it has unsaved changes; saving clears it, and closing a tab only asks for confirmation when it actually has unsaved changes. Saving a snippet that was opened from the tree overwrites it. Saving a new, unnamed tab opens a menu instead: New Snippet (asks for a name and saves it at the top level), OVERWRITE … for each existing snippet, and a submenu for every folder with the same choices inside it. Overwriting an existing snippet asks for confirmation first.

Keyboard shortcuts in the Snippets section (they can be changed under Settings > Shortcuts > Snippets):

| Action | Windows/Linux | Mac |
|---|---|---|
| Save Snippet | Ctrl-S | Command-S |
| New Snippet | Ctrl-N | Command-N |
| Close Snippet Tab | Ctrl-W | Command-W |

**Using snippets from a Query or Console tab**

Right-click inside the editor of a Query or Console tab:

- Save as snippet saves the editor's text as a snippet, using the same menu as above (a new snippet, or overwrite an existing one, in any folder);
- Use snippet (shown once you have at least one snippet) inserts the chosen snippet's text at the cursor.

---

# Visualizing Query Plans
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/visualizing_query_plans.html

**Full Content:**

OmniDB has a very useful feature: graphical query plan visualization. This may come in handy when writing or optimizing queries, since it allows you to easily identify performance bottlenecks in your SQL query.

For this feature, SQL Query inner tab shows 2 buttons: Explain and Explain Analyze.

**Textual visualization**

When you click the Explain button, OmniDB will execute an `EXPLAIN` command in your query. Initial visualization is textual and will show exactly the output of the `EXPLAIN` command, but with colored bars representing the estimated cost. The higher the cost, the darker and wider the bar.

When you click the Explain Analyze button, OmniDB will execute an `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` command in your query. Beware that this command will really execute the query. Also, the textual visualization will show much more information, and the costs are not estimated as in those provided by the `EXPLAIN` command; they are real costs.

**Tree visualization**

Both Explain and Explain Analyze modes also can graphically represent the textual output into a tree diagram. Each circle represent a node executed by the query plan, and the larger the circle, the higher the cost.

When queries become more and more complex, also its query plan can be very complex. With such queries (like the check bloat query we executed below) the tree visualization can be very interesting:

The query plan visualization component allows you to easily switch between textual and 2 tree visualizations, which can be zoomed in and out.

---

# Visualizing Data
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/visualizing_data.html

**Full Content:**

This feature displays a graph with nodes representing tables and edges representing table relationships with foreign keys. Using the mouse, the user is able to zoom in, zoom out, and drag and drop nodes to change its position.

There are two types of graphs: Simple Graph and Complete Graph.

**Simple graph**

This one display simple table nodes and their relationships. To access it just right click the schema node you want in the tree and then select the action Render Graph > Simple Graph:

**Complete graph**

This graph displays tables with all its columns and respective data types. To access it just right click the schema you want in the tree and then select the action Render Graph > Complete Graph:

# Managing other Elements
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/managing_other_elements.html

**Full Content:**

All PostgreSQL structures are possible to be managed with the use of SQL templates. This gives the user more power than using graphical forms to manipulate structures.

For example, let's consider the sequences inside the schema `public` of the database `ds2`. To create a new sequence, right click on the Sequences node, and choose Create Sequence.

After you change the name of the sequence, you can uncomment other command options and set them accordingly to your needs. When the entire command looks fine, just execute it and the new sequence will be created:

With right click on an existing sequence, you can alter or drop it. It will work the same way as the creation, by using a SQL template for the user to change.
