# Additional Features
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/additional_features.html

**Full Content:**

This chapter collects smaller features that don't need a chapter of their own. Several features that used to be described here now have their own chapters: Settings and Languages, Snippets, Notify, Connected Users (which replaces the former Backends tree menu) and Roles and Permissions.

**The Welcome page**

The Welcome icon at the top of the left rail opens a start page with the Getting started button, a reminder that most actions talk directly to the database you are connected to (so practice on a test environment rather than production), links to the OmniDB website, the GitHub repository and this documentation, and the version you are running.

**Getting Started tutorial**

The lightbulb icon near the bottom of the rail (Getting Started; in the desktop app also Help > Getting Started) opens a list of interactive walkthroughs that highlight the relevant parts of the screen step by step: creating an OmniDB user (server version only), creating a database connection, creating a terminal connection, meeting the snippets panel, using a connection and the connection tab (available once a connection is open). End walkthrough leaves a walkthrough at any time.

**Contextual Help**

Most of tree nodes (generally grouping ones like Schemas or Tables) offer contextual help. This feature can be accessed by right-clicking the tree node. When you click the Doc: … option, OmniDB opens the specific page of the online PostgreSQL Documentation in your web browser (the system's default browser in the desktop app, or a new tab when running as a browser-based OmniDB Server). It also picks the right documentation version for the PostgreSQL server you are connected to.

**Properties and DDL**

By clicking on most of objects in the tree view (tables, sequences, views, roles, databases, etc), the user will be able to see a very comprehensive list of properties of the object.

In the other panel called DDL, the user will be able to see the SQL DDL source code that can be used to re-create the object — including its comment (`COMMENT ON …`) and privileges (`GRANT …`) where the database has them. The user can copy this text and paste it wherever he/she wants.

The divider above the Properties/DDL panel can be dragged, and the panel (as well as the database tree itself) can be collapsed with the small toggle button on its divider — in the desktop app also with View > Toggle Properties/DDL Panel and View > Toggle Database Tree.

**Export Data**

The Query Tab can save the results of its query to a CSV, TSV, XLSX, JSON, XML or Markdown file. Pick the format in the drop-down next to the Export Data button and click the button: OmniDB runs the query again in the background and writes the whole result to the file (the export can be cancelled while it runs).

- In the desktop app, a native Save As dialog opens so you can choose where to save the file, and OmniDB confirms with File exported to: ….
- In the browser (server version), the result area shows The file is ready. with a Save link that downloads it.

CSV and TSV files use the encoding set in Settings > Export > CSV/TSV Encoding (default: UTF-8 with BOM), and CSV files the CSV Delimiter set there (default `;`). Export files are kept in a temporary folder inside OmniDB's home directory, can only be downloaded by the user who created them, and are removed automatically after 24 hours.

**Export as DBML**

Right-click a database node in the PostgreSQL tree and choose Export as DBML to generate the whole database's schema as a DBML (https://dbml.dbdiagram.io/home/) (Database Markup Language) document — every table, column, data type, primary key, unique and foreign-key constraint, index and comment — via a single pure-SQL introspection query adapted from the pg_dbml (https://pg_dbml.80.cz) project.

DBML is a compact, plain-text schema format, which makes it a good fit for giving an LLM/AI assistant context about your database: pasting a `.dbml` file into a chat is far cheaper in tokens than pasting a full SQL dump or having the model run its own introspection queries table by table, while still precisely describing every table, column, type and relationship.

The generated file defaults to `<database>.dbml`. In the desktop app this opens the native Save dialog, just like Export Data; in the browser (server) it shows a Download/Cancel prompt instead — Cancel discards the generated file right away rather than waiting for the temp folder's 24-hour cleanup. Currently PostgreSQL only.

**Query History**

From the Query Tab you can click on the Command history button to see a full, browsable and searchable list of the commands run on this connection, filterable by date range and text. See Writing SQL Queries.

**SSH Console**

Besides database connections, OmniDB can open a full-featured SSH terminal to a server. Create a connection of type Terminal in the Connections section, filling in the SSH server, port, user and password or private key (see Creating Users and Connections). Open it from the + at the end of the connection tab strip → SSH Consoles, or with Connect in its form. The terminal opens as its own connection tab; the server's host key must already be known — see Security and Multi-user Server.

---

# OmniDB Config Tool
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/omnidb_config_tool.html

**Full Content:**

Note: the standalone `omnidb-config`/`omnidb-config-app`/ `omnidb-config-server` CLI utility described on this page belonged to the previous Python/Django-based build and is not part of the current release. The single `omnidb-server` binary accepts only a handful of command-line options: `-A`/`--app` (desktop app mode), `-H`/`--host` (listening address), `-p`/`--port` (listening port), `-d`/`--homedir` (choose the home directory) and `--set-password` (set a user's password, see below) — all described in the Command options section of Deploying omnidb-server. There is no configuration file. The maintenance tasks the old tool offered can still be done manually, described below.

**Home directory**

OmniDB stores everything — the `omnidb.db` database (users, connections, and other app data) and a `temp` folder for exported files — in a single home directory. By default this is `~/.omnidb/omnidb-app` (desktop mode) or `~/.omnidb/omnidb-server` (server mode); pass `-d /some/path` to use a different one (the directory must already exist). If the operating system offers no secret store for the encryption key of saved passwords, the same directory also holds that key, in the file `.connection_secret_key` — see Security and Multi-user Server. When you back up or move `omnidb.db`, take that file along too.

**Create a user**

There is currently no CLI option to create a user without opening OmniDB. On first run against an empty home directory, OmniDB creates a default `admin` superuser automatically — in server mode with a random password printed once to the server's log output (the line containing `initial login: admin / …`). Sign in with it and create further users under Settings > Account > Manage Users, or change the password under Settings > Password.

**Set or reset a password**

If the one-time initial `admin` password was lost (or you want to set your own before the first sign-in), set the password of any existing user directly in the app database, without starting the server:

```
user@machine:~$ omnidb-server --set-password admin
user@machine:~$ omnidb-server --set-password admin -d /path/to/homedir
```

Without `-d` it uses the default server home directory (`~/.omnidb/omnidb-server`). In a terminal it asks for the new password twice, without echoing it; otherwise it reads the password from the first line of standard input, which is handy in scripts:

```
user@machine:~$ printf '%s\n' "$PW" | omnidb-server --set-password admin
```

The password is never passed as a command-line argument, so it doesn't end up in `ps` output or the shell history. It must be at least 8 characters long, and the user must already exist. The option is refused together with `-A` — the desktop app signs in automatically and has no password to manage. It can also be run while the server is running: the new password works immediately for new sign-ins, while users who are already signed in stay signed in until their session expires or the server restarts.

**Vacuum**

OmniDB has a single SQLite database, `omnidb.db`, storing all users, connections, and other OmniDB-related data. Since it's a plain SQLite file, you can vacuum it with any SQLite client while OmniDB isn't running, e.g.:

```
user@machine:~$ sqlite3 ~/.omnidb/omnidb-app/omnidb.db 'VACUUM;'
```

**Reset database**

If you wish to wipe out all OmniDB information and get a clean database as it was just installed, quit OmniDB and delete (or move aside) the home directory's `omnidb.db` file. A new, empty one — with a fresh default `admin` user (in server mode with a newly generated one-time password printed to the log) — is created automatically the next time OmniDB starts. Use this with caution: it cannot be undone.

**Delete temporary files**

Exported query results (CSV/XLSX/etc.) are written to the `temp` folder inside the home directory. It's safe to delete its contents manually at any time while OmniDB isn't running; OmniDB re-creates it as needed.

---

# Writing PL/pgSQL Functions
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/writing_plpgsql_functions.html

**Full Content:**

**Introduction**

PostgreSQL is more than a RDBMS engine. It is a developing platform. It provides a very powerful and flexible programming language called `PL/pgSQL`. Using this language you can write your own user-defined functions to achieve abstraction levels and procedural calculations that would be difficult to achieve with plain SQL (and sometimes impossible to achieve without context-switching with the application).

**Writing functions**

In the `public` schema, right-click the `Functions` node and click on Create Function. It will open a SQL Query inner tab, already containing a SQL Template to help you create your first PL/pgSQL function.

You can refer to PostgreSQL documentation on how to write user-defined functions. Just right-click the Functions node and click on Doc: Functions — the relevant PostgreSQL documentation page opens in your web browser (the system's default browser in the desktop app, or a new tab when running as a browser-based OmniDB Server).

For now, let us replace this SQL template entirely for the source code below:

```
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.fnc_count_vowels (p_input text)
RETURNS integer LANGUAGE plpgsql AS
$function$
DECLARE
  str text;
  ret integer;
  i   integer;
  len integer;
BEGIN
  str := upper(p_input);
  ret := 0;
  i := 1;
  len := length(p_input);
  WHILE i <= len LOOP
    IF substr(str, i, 1) in ('A', 'E', 'I', 'O', 'U') THEN
      ret := ret + 1;
    END IF;
    i := i + 1;
  END LOOP;
  RETURN ret;
END;
$function$
```

This will create a function called `fnc_count_vowels` inside the schema `public`. This function takes a text argument called `p_input` and counts how many vowels there are in this string. Then returns this count.

To create the function, execute the command in the SQL Query inner tab. If successful, the function will appear under the Functions tree node (you can refresh it by right-clicking and then clicking in Refresh). By expanding the function node as well, you can see its return type and its argument.

Now let us execute this new function for the first time. Open a simple SQL Query inner tab and execute the following SQL query:

```
SELECT public.fnc_count_vowels('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.')
```

Note how the query returns a single value, containing the number of vowels in the text.

By right-clicking the function node, you can see there are actions to edit, select and drop it. As you probably guessed, each action will open SQL Query inner tabs with handy SQL templates in them.

---

# Monitoring Dashboard
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/monitoring_dashboard.html

**Full Content:**

The Monitoring section is a live dashboard of charts and grids for the server behind a connection — transaction rate, backends, WAL production, database size, cache hit ratios and more — built from small, independent cards called Monitoring Units. Besides the units that come with OmniDB you can write your own, each one a single SQL query.

Built-in units exist for PostgreSQL (16 units) and MySQL (1 unit, Thread Count). MariaDB and Oracle connections get the dashboard too, for your own custom units. For other engines the section shows Monitoring is not supported for … connections.

**Opening the dashboard**

Click the Monitoring icon in the left rail (between Database and Notify). The dashboard belongs to a connection that is open in the Database section: the strip of open connection tabs is shown at the top of the section, and selecting a tab shows that connection's dashboard. With no connection open it shows No connection open.

All units start paused when the dashboard loads, so opening it does not start querying the server by itself. Start the ones you want with their own play button, or all of them at once with Enable All.

**The toolbar**

The toolbar at the top stays in place while the cards scroll below it:

- the first, icon-only button (tooltip Manage Units) opens or closes the unit list side panel, described below;
- Refresh All refreshes every shown unit once;
- Enable All / Pause All start or stop the automatic refresh of every unit of this connection;
- Card size — Small, Medium, Large or Full width — sets how wide a card may get before the grid wraps to fewer columns: a narrow window shows one card per row, a wide monitor several side by side. The choice is remembered in your browser.

**A Monitoring Unit card**

Each card has its title at the top, a × that removes (hides) the unit from the dashboard, and — for your own custom units — an edit button that opens its editor (both appear when you hover the card). Below the title are the unit's controls: refresh now, pause / play, and the refresh interval in seconds. The rest of the card is the unit's chart or grid.

A unit is one of three types:

- Grid: runs its query on each refresh and shows the result as a data grid.
- Chart (No Append): redraws a complete chart on each refresh; the previous values are replaced. Best for pie or doughnut charts of a current state.
- Timeseries: appends a new set of values to its chart on each refresh, keeping the most recent points, so you can watch a value develop over time. All built-in units are timeseries.

**Managing units**

The Manage Units side panel (toggled by the toolbar's first button, and resizable by dragging its edge) lists every unit available for the connection:

- the checkbox in front of a unit shows or hides it on the dashboard (hiding stops it, the same as its card's ×, but keeps its refresh interval for next time);
- drag a row up or down to change the order of the cards on the dashboard;
- the + below the list opens the New Unit editor;
- for a custom unit, right-click → Edit or Delete, or double-click it to open its editor. Built-in units cannot be edited or deleted, only shown or hidden.

Your custom units are private to your OmniDB user.

**Built-in units**

PostgreSQL: Transaction Rate, Backends, Autovacuum Workers Usage, WAL Production Rate, Temp Files Creation Rate, Autovacuum Freeze, Blocked Locks, Database Size, Database Growth Rate, Heap Cache Miss Ratio, Index Cache Miss Ratio, Seq Scan Ratio, Long Transaction, Long Query, Long Autovacuum and Checkpoints. MySQL: Thread Count. They need nothing extra installed in the database.

**Writing custom Monitoring Units**

A custom unit is a single SQL query that runs on a timer — with the same connection and permissions your SQL editor has. There is no separate scripting language to learn.

Note: since the query re-runs unattended, only `SELECT` (or `WITH ... SELECT`) queries are accepted — a destructive statement pasted in by mistake is rejected outright rather than silently firing on a timer.

Click + in the Manage Units panel. A Monitor Unit editor tab opens with the fields Name, Type (Timeseries, Chart (No Append) or Grid), Refresh Interval (seconds), Template (optionally start from an existing unit), Chart Type (Bar, Pie, Doughnut or Line; shown for Chart (No Append) only) and the SQL Query editor.

The query's shape depends on the unit's type:

Grid: no particular shape — whatever columns and rows the query returns become the grid. For example:

```
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity
```

Chart (No Append): one row per category — the first column is the label, the remaining column(s) are one series each (the column name becomes the series name). For example, a pie chart of database sizes:

```
SELECT datname,
       round(pg_catalog.pg_database_size(datname) / 1048576.0, 2) AS size_mb
FROM pg_catalog.pg_database
WHERE datname NOT IN ('template0', 'template1')
```

Timeseries: exactly one row — each numeric column becomes one continuously-appended series. For example, tracking the total database size over time:

```
SELECT round(sum(pg_catalog.pg_database_size(datname)) / 1048576.0, 2) AS total_size_mb
FROM pg_catalog.pg_database
WHERE NOT datistemplate
```

Click Test to run the query once and see the result rendered below the editor — as many times as you like. When you are happy with it, give the unit a name, set the refresh interval and click Save. The unit then appears in the Manage Units list; tick it to show it on the dashboard.

---

# Notify
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/notify.html

**Full Content:**

The Notify section listens for asynchronous notifications that sessions send through the database itself, and shows them as they arrive:

- PostgreSQL: `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY`;
- Oracle: `DBMS_ALERT`;
- Firebird: events (`POST_EVENT`).

MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server and SQLite have no equivalent; for them the section says NOTIFY-style channels are not supported for … connections. instead of hiding the feature.

**Opening the section**

Click the Notify icon in the left rail. The section shares the strip of open connection tabs with the Database section — select a tab to see that connection's channels and messages. With no connection open it shows No connection open. and asks you to open one in the Database panel first.

Listening does not depend on the Notify section being visible: as soon as a connection is opened in the Database section, OmniDB starts listening on its saved channels (over a separate, dedicated connection, so it never interferes with your Query or Console tabs), and it stops when that connection tab is closed.

**Channels**

The left side of the section is a tree with a Channels root. To add a channel, click + below the tree (or right-click the tree → Add Channel), type the Channel Name and press Enter. OmniDB starts listening on it immediately. Oracle alert names are limited to 30 bytes, Firebird event names to 255.

Right-click a channel for:

- Pause / Resume — stop or restart listening on that channel (a paused channel shows a crossed-out bell);
- Clear Messages — remove that channel's messages from the list;
- Delete — remove the channel (also available as − below the tree), after confirmation. Its messages are removed too.

Channels and their paused/active state are saved per OmniDB user and per connection, so they come back after a restart. PostgreSQL channel names are used as quoted, case-sensitive identifiers.

**Messages**

Received messages appear on the right in a table with the columns Channel, Time (when OmniDB received it) and Payload. Firebird events carry no payload, so for them Payload shows how many times the event was posted.

The row of checkboxes above the table filters the list: All channels, or only the channels you tick. Clear All empties the whole list.

Messages are kept only in the browser (or desktop window) that received them: they are not stored anywhere and are gone after a page reload.

If messages arrive faster than the page consumes them, OmniDB stops listening rather than letting them pile up without limit; it also stops if the listening connection fails. In both cases a banner explains why, with a Restart Listening button.

**Sending a test notification**

Notifications are sent with plain SQL, for example from a Query tab on the same database:

```
-- PostgreSQL (delivered when the transaction commits)
NOTIFY my_channel, 'hello';
SELECT pg_notify('my_channel', 'hello');

-- PostgreSQL, channel name with upper-case letters: quote it
NOTIFY "MyChannel", 'hello';

-- Oracle
BEGIN
  DBMS_ALERT.SIGNAL('my_alert', 'hello');
  COMMIT;
END;

-- Firebird (the event is posted on commit)
EXECUTE BLOCK AS BEGIN POST_EVENT 'my_event'; END
```

---

# Connected Users
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/connected_users.html

**Full Content:**

The Connected Users section shows who is connected to a database server right now — PostgreSQL backends, MySQL/MariaDB threads, Oracle and SQL Server sessions, Firebird attachments — what each of them is doing, and lets you terminate one. It replaces the older per-engine Backends/Process List/Sessions entries of the database tree's context menu.

Supported: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and Firebird. SQLite has no such concept, and shows Viewing connected users is not supported for … connections.

**Opening the section**

Click the Connected Users icon in the left rail. Like Monitoring, Notify and Permissions, it works on a connection already open in the Database section: the strip of open connection tabs is shown at the top, and the list belongs to the selected tab. With no connection open it shows No connection open.

The list is loaded when you enter the section and whenever you switch to another connection tab; it does not refresh on its own. To reload it, right-click the grid and choose Refresh. The number of rows is shown above the grid (Number of records: …).

**Columns**

Columns are grouped compactly (for example an ID under a name, or address and port on one line); hovering a column header explains what it shows and which catalog column it comes from.

- PostgreSQL (`pg_stat_activity`): PID, Database, User, Client, Application, Process start / Transaction start, Query start / Last state change, Waiting on, State, Transaction ID, Query ID, Process type.
- MySQL/MariaDB (process list): User (with the connection ID), Host, Database, Command, Time (s), State.
- Oracle (`v$session`): SID (with Serial#), User, State, Schema, Client, Program, Module / action, Client info, Logon time, Idle (s), SQL ID, Waiting on, Blocking SID.
- SQL Server (user sessions): Session ID, Login name, Host, Program, State.
- Firebird (`mon$attachments`, without OmniDB's own attachment): Attachment ID, User, Remote address, State.

For PostgreSQL and Oracle, background/system processes are hidden by default; tick Show system processes above the grid to include them (the checkbox only appears when there are such rows).

**Viewing a session's query**

For PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, clicking a row opens a Query text pane below the grid with the statement that session is running (or ran last), syntax-highlighted and read-only. From there you can copy it, or use Open in a new Query tab to continue working with it in a regular Query tab, for example to run Explain on it.

**Terminating a session**

Right-click a row and choose Terminate. After you confirm, OmniDB ends that session the engine's own way — `pg_terminate_backend()` on PostgreSQL, `KILL` on MySQL/MariaDB and SQL Server, `ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION … IMMEDIATE` on Oracle, deleting the row from `mon$attachments` on Firebird — and reloads the list. This needs the matching privilege on the database server. The same context menu also offers Copy and View Content for the clicked cell.

---

# Roles and Permissions
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/permissions.html

**Full Content:**

The Permissions section is a role and privilege browser for PostgreSQL. It lays a server's roles out Finder-style, in side-by-side columns: pick a role on the left, and the columns to its right show who it is a member of, who is a member of it, and what it can actually do on every database object — including everything it only has indirectly, through inherited role memberships or through `PUBLIC`. Roles, memberships and privileges can be created, changed and revoked right there.

Note: this section currently supports PostgreSQL only. For any other connection it shows Permissions are not yet supported for … / Currently only PostgreSQL is supported.

**Opening the section**

Click the Permissions icon (the people icon) in the left rail. The section works on a connection that is already open in the Database section: the same strip of open connection tabs is shown at its top, and the section uses whichever connection tab is selected there. With no connection open it shows No connection open — open one first (see Managing Databases). The columns are rebuilt every time you enter the section, so any earlier selection is reset.

Everything you do here needs the same privileges the equivalent SQL would need (`CREATEROLE`, superuser, or ownership of the object, depending on the action) — OmniDB runs the statements with the credentials of the connection you are using.

**Column 1: Roles**

The Roles column lists every role on the server, including the built-in `pg_*` roles, sorted by name. Roles that can log in (users) have a single-person icon; roles that cannot (groups) have a two-person icon. The first row is always `PUBLIC` (globe icon) — not a real role, but the pseudo-role every role implicitly belongs to, so that privileges granted to `PUBLIC` can be browsed and edited the same way.

Click a role to focus it; the other columns then show that role. Below the list:

- + opens the Create Role dialog: Role name, Password, and the attribute checkboxes Can log in (on by default), Superuser, Can create databases, Can create roles, Inherits privileges of roles it is a member of (on by default), Can initiate replication and Bypasses row-level security, plus Connection limit (-1 = unlimited) and Account expires (leave empty for no expiration).
- − drops the selected role (disabled for `PUBLIC`).

Right-clicking a role (not `PUBLIC`) offers:

- Change Password — asks for the new password twice. The password is hashed in the format the server itself is configured for (SCRAM-SHA-256 or md5) before it is sent.
- Alter Attributes — the same attribute fields as Create Role, pre-filled with the role's current values. Clearing Account expires removes the expiration.
- Drop Role — asks Drop role "…"? This cannot be undone. and then runs a plain `DROP ROLE`; PostgreSQL refuses it while the role still owns objects or holds privileges.

**Column 2: memberships**

The second column is split in two halves:

- … — Members (top): the roles that are members of the focused role.
- … — Member of (bottom): every role the focused role belongs to, directly or through other roles, flattened into one list. `PUBLIC` is always listed first.

In both halves, direct memberships are shown in normal text and indirect (inherited) ones greyed out. A direct membership granted `WITH ADMIN OPTION` is marked (admin option). For `PUBLIC` both halves just say PUBLIC is not a member of any role.

- The + under Member of opens Grant Membership: pick a role to make the focused role a member of it, optionally With admin option.
- The + under Members opens Add Member: the same dialog the other way round — the picked role becomes a member of the focused role.
- − (or right-click → Remove Membership) revokes a membership after asking Revoke membership in "…"?. Only direct memberships can be removed; an inherited one has to be revoked where it is actually granted.
- Double-clicking a row, or right-click → Set as Active Role, makes that role the focused one, exactly as if you had clicked it in the Roles column — the quickest way to follow an inheritance chain upwards.

**Column 3: objects and effective privileges**

The third column, … — Objects, is a tree of everything the focused role has any privilege on — its effective privileges: its own direct grants plus everything it inherits through its memberships and through `PUBLIC`. It starts with two groups, Databases (every database on the server) and Tablespaces; a node is shown normally if the role has some privilege there, and greyed out otherwise.

Expanding a database loads its objects over a separate connection to that database (the connection tab's own active database does not change): schemas, and inside each schema folders for tables, views, sequences, functions, procedures, materialized views, types and domains; foreign data wrappers and foreign servers sit directly under the database. Only objects the role actually has a privilege on are listed (system schemas are left out); a schema shown greyed out is there only because something inside it is. If there is nothing at all, the database shows No privileges on any object in this database.

**Editing privileges**

Right-click a database, tablespace, schema or object and choose Edit Privileges. The dialog lists every privilege valid for that kind of object as a checkbox:

- database: `CREATE`, `CONNECT`, `TEMPORARY`; tablespace: `CREATE`; schema: `CREATE`, `USAGE`;
- table, view and materialized view: `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE`, `REFERENCES`, `TRIGGER`;
- sequence: `USAGE`, `SELECT`, `UPDATE`; function and procedure: `EXECUTE`; type, domain, foreign data wrapper and foreign server: `USAGE`.

Each checkbox tells you where the privilege comes from:

- checked — the role holds it directly; uncheck it to `REVOKE` it;
- checked but disabled, with Inherited from: … — the role only has it through another role or `PUBLIC`. It cannot be revoked here; make the source role active (Set as Active Role) and revoke it there;
- unchecked — the role does not have it; check it to `GRANT` it directly.

With grant option applies to the privileges you newly grant in that dialog. Confirm with the dialog's main button, which is labelled with the object's name.

To grant something on an object that is not in the tree yet, use the + (Add Object Privilege) under the column: choose the Object Type, then the Database (for everything except databases and tablespaces; it defaults to the connection's current database), the Schema for schema-level objects, the Object itself (functions are shown with their argument signature), tick the Privileges and, optionally, With grant option.

Selecting `PUBLIC` in the first column lets you edit what is granted to `PUBLIC` itself (`GRANT … TO PUBLIC` / `REVOKE … FROM PUBLIC`).

Important: every action in this section is executed on the server immediately — there is no SQL preview and no undo. Only Drop Role and Remove Membership ask for confirmation first. If the server rejects a statement, its error message is shown.

---

# Logical Replication
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/logical_replication.html

**Full Content:**

PostgreSQL 10 introduces native logical replication, which uses a publish/subscribe model and so we can create publications on the upstream (or publisher) and subscriptions on downstream (or subscriber). For more details about it, please refer to the PostgreSQL (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/10/static/sql-createpublication.html) documentation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/10/static/sql-createsubscription.html).

In this chapter, we will use a 2-node cluster to demonstrate PostgreSQL 10 native logical replication. Note that on each PostgreSQL instance, you need to configure `wal_level = logical` and also make sure to adjust file `pg_hba.conf` to grant access to `replication` between the 2 nodes.

**Creating a test environment**

Set up two PostgreSQL 10+ instances however you prefer (Docker, a virtual machine, or even two databases on the same machine) and configure the settings above on each.

**Connecting to both nodes**

Let's use OmniDB to connect to both PostgreSQL nodes. First of all, fill out connection info in the Connections section:

Then select both connections. Note how OmniDB understands it is connected to PostgreSQL 10 and enables a new node in the current connection tree view: it is called Logical Replication. Inside of it, we can see Publications and Subscriptions.

**Creating a test table on both nodes**

On both nodes, create a table like this:

```
CREATE TABLE customers (
 login text PRIMARY KEY,
 full_name text NOT NULL,
 registration_date timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
)
```

**Create a publication on the first machine**

Inside the connection node, expand the Logical Replication node, then right click in the Publications node, and choose the action Create Publication. OmniDB will open a SQL template tab with the `CREATE PUBLICATION` command ready for you to make some adjustments and run:

After adjusting and executing the command, you can right click the Publications node again and click on the Refresh action. You will see that will be created a new node with the same name you gave to the publication. Expanding this node, you will see the details and the tables for the publication:

**Create a subscription on the second machine**

Inside the connection node, expand the Logical Replication node, then right click in the Subscriptions node, and choose the action Create Subscription. OmniDB will open a SQL template tab with the `CREATE SUBSCRIPTION` command ready for you to make some adjustments and run:

After adjusting and executing the command, you can right click the Subscriptions node again and click on the Refresh action. You will see that will be created a new node with the same name you gave to the subscription. Expanding this node, you will see the details, the referenced publications and the tables for the subscription:

Also, the `CREATE SUBSCRIPTION` command created a logical replication slot called `testsub` (the same name as the subscription) in the first machine:

**Testing the logical replication**

To test the replication is working, let's create some data on the node 1. Right click on the table `public.customers`, then point to Data Actions, then click on the action Edit Data. In this grid, you are able to add, edit and remove data from the table. Add 2 sample rows, like this:

Then, on the other node, check if the table `public.customers` was automatically populated. Right click on the table `public.customers`, then point to Data Actions, then click on the action Query Data:

As we can see, both rows created in the first machine were replicated into the second machine. This tell us that the logical replication is working.

Now you can perform other actions, such as adding/removing tables to the publication and creating a new publication that publishes all tables.

# Deploying omnidb-server
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/deploying_omnidb-server.html

**Full Content:**

Note: since the 3.6.x rewrite, `omnidb-server` is a single native binary (no separate webserver/websocket-server pair, no Django/CherryPy/Tornado) that answers every request itself over one port, using long-polling rather than websockets for background query/console/monitoring updates. There is also no configuration file or built-in TLS support anymore — everything is set via command-line flags, and any TLS termination must be handled by a reverse proxy in front of it.

**Command options**

```
Usage: omnidb-server [options]

Options:
  -A, --app              run in desktop app mode (always binds loopback-only,
                          regardless of -H)
  -H HOST, --host=HOST   listening address (default: 127.0.0.1)
  -p PORT, --port=PORT   listening port (default: an OS-chosen free port)
  -d HOMEDIR, --homedir=HOMEDIR
                         home directory containing the omnidb.db database and
                         the temp folder used for exported files
      --set-password=USER
                         set USER's password in the app database and exit
                         (prompts for it; does not start the server)
```

- `-H` specifies the address to listen on. Defaults to `127.0.0.1` (loopback-only) — pass `0.0.0.0` to accept connections from other machines, or a specific interface address.
- `-p` specifies the port to listen on, used in the browser's URL when accessing OmniDB directly. If omitted, the OS picks a free port and prints it to stderr on startup. Since that port changes on every start, always pass `-p` for a server other people (or a reverse proxy) connect to.
- `-d` lets you choose the folder that stores `omnidb.db` (the application database) and the `temp` folder used for exported files. The folder must already exist; without `-d`, `~/.omnidb/omnidb-server` is used (created automatically). With this option it's possible to run several instances of `omnidb-server`, each pointing at a different directory — handy for Docker deployments where you mount a volume there.
- `--set-password USER` sets an existing user's password directly in the app database and exits without starting the server — see OmniDB Config Tool.

Security note: a server started with `-H` set to anything other than loopback should never also be started with `-A`/`--app` — the desktop auto-login link that mode generates is only meant to be reachable locally, so `-A` always forces loopback binding regardless of `-H`, ignoring it entirely rather than risk that combination.

On startup the server prints the address to open, for example `omnidb-server: listening on 127.0.0.1:9000 — open http://127.0.0.1:9000/omnidb_login/ in your browser`. The very first start against an empty home directory also prints the one-time password of the initial `admin` user — see Security and Multi-user Server, which also describes what a multi-user server restricts and protects. Stop the server with Ctrl-C (or `SIGTERM`); it shuts down gracefully.

Let's take a look on how to deploy `omnidb-server` in different scenarios:

**Deploying OmniDB directly**

Running `omnidb-server` with `-H 0.0.0.0` (or a specific public interface) makes it directly reachable from other machines — but since there is no built-in TLS support, this means plain, unencrypted HTTP. This is not recommended for anything beyond a trusted local network: session cookies and query results would otherwise travel in the clear. For anything reachable from the wider internet, put a TLS-terminating reverse proxy (see below) in front instead of exposing `omnidb-server` directly.

**Deploying OmniDB behind a reverse proxy**

The recommended approach: run `omnidb-server` listening only on `127.0.0.1` (the default, so `-H` can be omitted) and let a reverse proxy such as Nginx (https://nginx.org) or Caddy (https://caddyserver.com) handle TLS termination and forward plain HTTP to it locally.

```
./omnidb-server -p 9000
```

Example Nginx configuration:

```
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;
    include snippets/ssl-domain.conf;
    include snippets/ssl-params.conf;
    server_name domain.org;
    client_max_body_size 75M;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:9000;
        proxy_set_header   X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header   X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header   X-Forwarded-Ssl https;
        proxy_set_header   X-Forwarded-Proto https;
        proxy_set_header   X-Forwarded-Port 443;
        proxy_set_header   Host localhost:9000;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
    }
}
```

Note the `Host` header: while `omnidb-server` listens on loopback, it only answers requests addressed to `127.0.0.1:<port>`, `localhost:<port>` or `[::1]:<port>` (anything else gets `421 Misdirected Request`) — a protection against DNS-rebinding attacks. The proxy therefore has to forward the request with `Host` set to the local address, as above, rather than passing the public host name through. Keep `X-Forwarded-Proto https`: it tells OmniDB to mark its session cookies `Secure`.

Since everything (including background query/console updates) is served over plain HTTP long-polling rather than websockets, a single `location /` block covering the whole app is all that's needed — there's no separate websocket upgrade path or `/wss` pattern to route specially anymore.

---

# Security and Multi-user Server
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/security.html

**Full Content:**

This chapter collects what OmniDB does to protect saved credentials and a shared, multi-user server, and what that means for you as an administrator or user. For installing and exposing the server see Deploying omnidb-server; for command-line password management see OmniDB Config Tool.

“Server mode” below means `omnidb-server` started without `-A` — a multi-user instance people sign in to from a browser, whether it listens on loopback only or on a network address (`-H`). The desktop app is always single-user.

**Saved passwords are encrypted**

Database passwords saved in a connection, SSH passwords/passphrases and SSH private keys are encrypted (AES-256-GCM) before they are written to OmniDB's user database, `omnidb.db`. The encryption key is not stored in that file: it is kept in the operating system's secret store — the macOS Keychain, the Windows Credential Manager or the Linux Secret Service — so a copy of `omnidb.db` alone does not reveal them.

Where no secret store is reachable (typically a headless Linux server), OmniDB keeps the key in a file named `.connection_secret_key` (readable by its owner only) in the OmniDB home directory instead; once that file exists it is always used. In that case:

- back the key file up together with `omnidb.db`, and protect both equally;
- if the key is lost, the stored secrets cannot be recovered — the connections still exist, but their passwords and SSH keys have to be entered again.

Existing unencrypted entries from older versions are encrypted automatically the first time a newer version starts. If you would rather not store a password at all, leave it empty in the connection form: OmniDB then asks for it when needed and keeps it only in memory, for 30 minutes, for your session (see Creating Users and Connections).

**The initial `admin` account**

A new server-mode installation creates one superuser, `admin`, with a random password that is printed once to the server's log output:

```
omnidb-server: initialized a new app database — initial login: admin / <password> (shown only once; change it under Settings, or run: omnidb-server --set-password admin)
```

Sign in with it and change it under Settings > Password, or set a password of your choice beforehand from the command line:

```
omnidb-server --set-password admin [-d /path/to/homedir]
```

The desktop app never shows a sign-in page; it signs in to its own local, loopback-only server automatically.

**Sign-in protection and sessions**

- After 10 failed sign-in attempts for the same user name, or from the same client address, within 15 minutes, further attempts are refused with Too many failed sign-in attempts. Please try again in 15 minutes. The counters are kept in memory and reset when the server restarts. Behind a reverse proxy the client address is the proxy's address.
- Deleting a user ends all of that user's sessions immediately, and removing superuser status takes effect immediately. Changing a password (in Settings or with `--set-password`) applies to new sign-ins at once; a password changed in Settings also signs out that user's other sessions.

**Restrictions in server mode**

Because every connection of a multi-user server is opened by the server process, on the server machine, some connection options that would read the server's own files are restricted:

- SQLite connections (a SQLite database is a file on the server) can only be created and used by OmniDB superusers. They cannot point inside OmniDB's own home directory, and `file:` URIs are rejected.
- PostgreSQL connection strings may not use the parameters `passfile`, `servicefile`, `service`, `sslkey`, `sslcert`, `sslrootcert`, `sslcrl` or `sslcrldir`.

These restrictions do not apply to the desktop app, where the files are your own.

**Public connections**

A connection marked Public connection? can be used by every OmniDB user on the server, but only its owner can edit it. For everyone else:

- the saved password is never sent to their browser, and a password embedded in the connection string is shown masked;
- Test Connection always tests the stored server, port and database — changing those fields in the form first does not redirect the stored password somewhere else.

**Exported files**

Query exports and DBML exports are written to the server's `temp` folder under random names and can only be downloaded by the user who created them. They are deleted automatically after 24 hours.

**SSH host keys**

SSH tunnels and SSH terminal connections verify the server's host key against the `~/.ssh/known_hosts` file of the operating-system user running `omnidb-server`. An unknown or changed host key is refused — OmniDB does not silently trust a host on first use. Add the host once from that account, for example:

```
ssh user@ssh-server.example.com        # accept the key once
# or
ssh-keyscan ssh-server.example.com >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts
```

**Network exposure**

There is no built-in TLS. Keep `omnidb-server` on `127.0.0.1` (the default) behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy rather than exposing plain HTTP with `-H 0.0.0.0` — see Deploying omnidb-server. While bound to loopback, the server only answers requests addressed to `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` or `[::1]` with its own port, which protects it against DNS-rebinding attacks from web pages. Session cookies are marked `Secure` when the request arrives over TLS or with `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`, and all state-changing requests are protected against cross-site request forgery.

---

# Console Tab
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/console_tab.html

**Full Content:**

The Console Tab provides an easy and comfortable way to interact with your databases. Users familiar with the `psql` command line utility will recognize the general shape — a scrollback log plus an input editor — and a useful subset of its backslash commands work here too:

- `\?`: show the command list;
- `\dt`: list tables;
- `\d`: list tables, views and sequences; `\d NAME` describes one of them (its columns, types, nullability and defaults) — `NAME` can be schema-qualified (`\d public.customers`);
- `\du`: list roles/users;
- `\l`: list databases;
- `\df`: list functions;
- `\x`: toggle expanded/vertical output;
- `\timing`: toggle showing execution time.

These map to whatever each connected engine actually has: MySQL/MariaDB's “database” doubles as its schema, Oracle's “user” doubles as its schema (and it has no separate multi-database concept), and SQLite has none of schemas/roles/databases at all — where an engine genuinely has nothing to show, the command says so directly instead of returning an empty or misleading result. `\h` (per-SQL-command syntax help, like a PostgreSQL manual page) is not implemented.

The editor on the bottom of the tab area is full-featured just like the Query Tab editor (it provides syntax highlight and autocomplete with Ctrl-Space, Option-Space on macOS, and its right-click menu offers Save as snippet and Use snippet). To execute a command, just type it in this editor. If the command is a backslash (starts with `\`), just type `Enter` and it will be executed. If it is a regular SQL command, then it can be multi-lined, and you will need to press Alt-Q (Ctrl-Q on macOS) to execute it.

All commands and its output will be logged into the display area, which is textual and read-only, so you can copy and paste its contents somewhere else. You can clear the display area by clicking on the Clear Console button.

All commands also are logged in the connection query history, and also in a local console history, which you can by clicking in the Command History button.

By clicking in the green check, you can borrow the command and put it into the editor, so you can amend it and execute it. Another comfortable way to navigate through the history is using the shortcuts Ctrl-Up and Ctrl-Down, to quickly paste in the editor the previous and next commands, respectively.

These backslash commands are useful when dealing with databases every day. The console tab will also show any errors and the results of any SQL command you type in a pretty way. Try it out!

---

# Editor Keyboard Shortcuts

OmniDB's SQL editor, Console editor and DDL/Properties viewer are all built on the Ace code editor (https://ace.c9.io/), which ships with its own rich set of keyboard shortcuts for editing, selecting and navigating text. This chapter lists them for reference. These are separate from OmniDB's own app-level shortcuts (Run Query, Cancel Query, switching tabs, etc.), which are listed with their defaults, and can be changed, under Settings > Shortcuts — see Settings and Languages.

# Legacy Features & History
URL: https://www.omnidb.net/en/legacy_features_and_history.html

**Full Content:**

OmniDB has gone through several very different lives — a university project, a Python/Django web app with a plugin ecosystem, and now a single-binary Go application. This page is the place for anything that used to exist but doesn't anymore: what it was, why it isn't coming back, and where to find it if you still need it. For the story of the project itself, see Introduction.

**Version timeline**

| Era | What it was |
|---|---|
| Original (ASP.NET/C#) | Undergrad final project at the Federal University of Paraná — the first tool to trace a common line between PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, Oracle, SQLite, Firebird and SQL Server metadata. |
| OmniDB (Python/Django) | The long-lived version most people know: a Django web app with a browser-based workspace and, from 2.9 onward, a Python plugin system for community extensions. Development on the original OmniDB/OmniDB (https://github.com/OmniDB/OmniDB) repository stopped around 2020. |
| 2025–2026 revival (3.1.x) | The project was picked back up: modernized codebase, improved security, native macOS Apple Silicon support, and a full documentation overhaul — still on the Python/Django backend at this point. |
| Go rewrite (3.6.x) | The entire backend was rewritten from Python/Django to Go and shipped as a single native binary. The Python runtime, and everything that only made sense inside it — including the plugin system — was removed. |
| Wails migration (done) | The desktop shell moved from NW.js to Wails (https://wails.io) (Go) — a smaller binary, no bundled Chromium, and the app now drives the OS's own native webview instead. |
| 4.x | New features on the Go codebase: MS SQL Server support back, the Notify, Monitoring, Connected Users and Permissions sections, a redesigned Connections and Settings UI, a multi-language interface, `.pgpass` support, encrypted saved passwords and a hardened multi-user server. |

**The plugin system (removed)**

The plugin system has been removed as part of the 3.6.x rewrite of the backend from Python/Django to Go, and is no longer available.

OmniDB 2.9 introduced a plugin system that let users write Python code, hooked into different parts of the interface, to add their own features without redeploying the whole application. That mechanism depended on dynamically importing arbitrary Python modules into the running server process — something with no equivalent in a compiled Go binary — and was deliberately not carried over. Since it could never do anything useful again, the “Plugins” dialog and its menu entry, and the API endpoints behind it, were removed from the application entirely rather than kept around as a permanently-empty stub.

If you relied on a specific plugin, there is currently no supported way to port it forward. Anything a plugin used to do by calling into the database directly can usually still be done today through the regular SQL editor, snippets, or a custom monitoring unit.

**PL/pgSQL step debugger (removed)**

OmniDB 2.3.0 added an interactive step debugger for PL/pgSQL functions and procedures — breakpoints, live variable inspection, and per-line execution statistics. It depended on a custom PostgreSQL C extension (`omnidb_plugin`) hooking into PL/pgSQL's internal plugin API, loaded via `shared_preload_libraries` (a server restart), plus a dedicated `omnidb` schema and passwordless local access for a second, debugger-only database connection.

The debugger has been removed, along with its “Debug Function”/“Debug Procedure” tree menu entries. It was never ported during the 3.6.x Go rewrite, and the `omnidb_plugin` extension itself hasn't been touched since 2020. Beyond the ongoing cost of keeping a PostgreSQL-internals C extension working across every new major PostgreSQL version, it fundamentally can't work at all against any managed/cloud PostgreSQL (RDS, Cloud SQL, Supabase, Neon, and similar) — none of them allow a custom `shared_preload_libraries` entry — so a large and growing share of today's users could never have used it regardless of how well it was maintained.

Writing and running PL/pgSQL functions themselves is unaffected — see Writing PL/pgSQL Functions. If you need to step through PL/pgSQL execution against your own self-hosted PostgreSQL server, the original `omnidb_plugin` source is still available in the original repository's history (https://github.com/OmniDB/OmniDB/tree/master/omnidb_plugin), or you can use pldebugger (https://github.com/EnterpriseDB/pldebugger) (the actively-maintained equivalent used by pgAdmin) directly, outside of OmniDB.

**Advanced Object Search (removed)**

Advanced Object Search let users apply pattern matching — the SQL `LIKE` operator, or a full regular expression — across database object names and table data, searching across several tables in parallel and opening a ready-made query tab for any match found.

Advanced Object Search has been removed. Its tree context-menu entry had already been commented out, and its frontend and backend code called functions that no longer exist anywhere in this codebase's history — it was never carried over during the 3.6.x rewrite from Python/Django to Go, and has not been reachable or functional since. The dead code has now been deleted outright rather than kept as a menu entry that could never work.

There is no supported replacement today. A `LIKE` or regular-expression search across specific tables or columns can still be written by hand in the regular SQL editor — see Writing SQL Queries.

**pglogical (removed)**

pglogical (https://www.2ndquadrant.com/en/resources/pglogical/) was a PostgreSQL extension providing an efficient logical-replication system. The old `omnidb-pglogical` plugin added tree-view nodes and SQL-template actions (create node, manage replication sets, create subscriptions, and so on) for working with it — all built on the removed plugin system above, so it no longer loads.

**Postgres-BDR (removed)**

Postgres-BDR (https://www.2ndquadrant.com/en/resources/bdr/) (“Bi-Directional Replication”) was 2ndQuadrant's multi-master extension for PostgreSQL. The old `omnidb-bdr` plugin gave it the same kind of tree-view integration as pglogical. Same story: it was a plugin, and the plugin system it depended on is gone.

**Postgres-XL (removed)**

Postgres-XL (https://www.2ndquadrant.com/en/resources/postgres-xl/) was a massively-parallel, horizontally-scalable fork of PostgreSQL (GTM + coordinator + data nodes). The old `omnidb-xl` plugin added cluster-aware tree-view nodes for it. Also a plugin, also gone.

**Why none of these are coming back**

All three were thin, plugin-based integrations for niche, largely unmaintained-upstream PostgreSQL forks/extensions — none of pglogical, BDR or Postgres-XL saw meaningful new releases in recent years. Rebuilding the plugin system itself in Go would mean designing an entirely new extension mechanism (compiled plugins, a scripting runtime, or a hook API) for a small and shrinking audience, which hasn't been a priority against the rest of the Go rewrite. Nothing about the rewrite prevents connecting to a pglogical/BDR/XL cluster as a plain PostgreSQL database and managing replication objects by hand through the regular SQL editor or Console tab — you simply don't get the dedicated tree-view nodes and SQL-template shortcuts the plugins used to add.

**Where to find the old releases**

Releases of classic OmniDB (up to ~2020) with full plugin support are still available, unmaintained, from the original repository:

- github.com/OmniDB/OmniDB (https://github.com/OmniDB/OmniDB) — the original application and its release archive.
- github.com/OmniDB/plugins (https://github.com/OmniDB/plugins) — the pglogical/BDR/XL plugin sources themselves.

Neither repository receives updates. If you need pglogical, BDR or Postgres-XL management today, an old release from there — run against a database matching its era — is your best option; there's no migration path from that setup into the current Go-based OmniDB.

---
